messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rajesh's Vigil

Rajesh Patel had returned from Syria eighteen months ago with a commendation letter and a wound he could not name. At thirty-five, he was a tax consultant in Chicago, a position that seemed, in the abstract planning of his recovery, perfectly suited to rebuilding a normal life—contained, predictable, numerical. His wife Priya had been relieved when he took the job. But the spreadsheets that once calmed him now became battlegrounds for his attention. Numbers would blur mid-calculation. He would find himself staring at a column of figures for ten minutes without registering a single entry, his mind elsewhere, reconstructing sequences of events that refused to arrange themselves in any coherent order.

The field hospital in Aleppo had been a converted school. Rajesh had been there as a medic with an international relief organization, one of four staff members managing a rotating schedule across three rooms. On the morning of March 14th, the building had been struck. He remembered the sound first—not the explosion itself, but the silence that followed it, a silence so complete it seemed to have weight. He remembered running toward the rubble, his body moving through doorways and past collapsed walls, stepping over things he would not allow himself to fully see. He remembered the smell, acrid and chemical, mixed with something else—burning flesh, burning fabric, burning everything—a smell that had entered his nostrils so completely that for weeks afterward he could taste it. He had found two colleagues in the second room, both dead. He had not been able to protect them. He had not even been in that room. The randomness of that fact—that he had stepped out moments before, that he had survived by accident—had corroded something foundational in how he understood the world. If survival was arbitrary, if protection was impossible, then what was the point of anything?

Now, when smoke drifted from a neighbor's barbecue, Rajesh's body seized. His hands would rise to his face, pressing hard against his eyes and nose as if he could unsee and unsmell the past. Priya had stopped inviting friends over. She had stopped suggesting they go anywhere, really. Last month, his mother had died—peacefully, at home, of natural causes—and the funeral had been unbearable. The cemetery itself was a trigger; the gathering of grief-stricken people was a trigger; even the gentle expressions of sympathy from relatives had felt like accusations. When his uncle had simply placed a hand on his shoulder, Rajesh had flinched so violently that he had knocked over a flower arrangement.

At work, his performance was declining. He had missed two client meetings because the thought of sitting in a conference room while someone—a colleague, a client—raised their voice in even mild frustration sent him into a state of hypervigilance that made concentration impossible. Any expression of anger, even a calmly stated disagreement, felt like an imminent threat. His manager had begun to notice. There had been a difficult conversation last week about his reliability.

The nights were the worst. Rajesh could not sleep past 3 a.m., and when he did sleep, his body would jolt awake at the smallest sound—the house settling, a car passing on the street, Priya shifting beside him. He felt safer during daylight, though safety was perhaps the wrong word. Daylight was merely less dangerous. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally chaotic, that people he cared about could be taken away without warning or reason, and that he was fundamentally alone in this knowledge. Priya tried to reach him, but he could not let her. To let her close felt like inviting her into the line of fire.

What had finally brought him to therapy was a moment of clarity that had terrified him more than the memories themselves. He had been sitting at his desk, unable to work, unable to think, and he had realized that he was avoiding everything that might make him feel better—he had turned down an invitation to his closest friend's engagement party, he had stopped the evening walks he used to take with Priya, he had even stopped calling his sister. He was, he understood with sudden certainty, disappearing. And the shame of that—the shame of having survived when others had not, the shame of being unable to protect anyone, the shame of being broken—was becoming too heavy to carry alone.
